pages.name: Where the curves cross
pages.text: A centrifugal pump gives its most head at no flow, and less as the flow grows. This example pump gives 30 − 0.04q² metres, with q in L/s. The pipe needs 10 + 0.06q² metres, its 10 m lift plus friction. That is its [[system curve]]. Where the two meet, the pump gives just what the pipe needs. That crossing is the [[operating point]]. Set them equal: 0.1q² = 20, so q² = 200. That is about 14.1 L/s at 22.0 m.
pages.alt: A graph of head against flow. The pump's curve falls from 30 m at no flow. The system curve rises from the 10 m lift. They cross at the operating point, about 14.1 L/s and 22.0 m.

pages.name: Spare head
pages.task: For a moment, the flow is 10 L/s. There the pump gives 30 − 4 = 26 m. The pipe needs only 10 + 6 = 16 m. What does the flow do next?
pages.why: The spare 10 m is an unbalanced push, so it speeds up the water in the pipe. The flow climbs until the two heads match, at about 14.1 L/s. Past the crossing, the pipe needs more than the pump gives, and the water slows. Either way, the flow comes back to the crossing.
pages.alt: A graph of head against flow, with the pump's curve and the system curve. At 10 L/s the pump gives 26 m and the pipe needs 16 m: 10 m are spare. The flow climbs to the crossing, about 14.1 L/s.

pages.name: Closing the valve
pages.text: A valve adds friction to the pipe. Each stop multiplies that friction, so the system curve bends up more steeply. The pump's curve stays put, so the crossing can only slide along it. At friction ×2 the pump settles at about 11.2 L/s and 25.0 m. Less water flows, at more head. The picture shows the valve at friction ×2.
pages.alt: A graph of head against flow, with the pump's curve and the system curve. A dot marks where they cross, the operating point, with dashed guides to the axes.

pages.name: The outlet gauge
pages.task: The outlet gauge sits between the pump and the valve. You close the valve a little. What happens to the flow and the gauge?
pages.why: The valve steepens the system curve. The crossing slides up the pump's curve, to less flow and more head. The gauge sits before the valve. It reads the suction pressure plus what the pump adds, so it rises with the pump's head.
pages.alt: A graph of head against flow: the pump's curve, the system curve with the valve open, and a dot where they cross. The valve at friction ×2 steepens the system curve, and the dot slides up the pump's curve to about 11.2 L/s and 25.0 m.

pages.name: Power as the valve closes
pages.text: The head rises a little while the flow falls a lot, so the pump does less work. The hump below is its [[efficiency]], the water's power ÷ the shaft's power. It peaks near 14 L/s, at about 71%. Pumps are chosen to run near that peak, like this one. Shut, the shaft's power is near its least, and so is the motor's current. The picture shows the valve shut.
pages.alt: A graph of head against flow, with the pump's curve and the system curve left out, as the valve is shut. No water flows, so the dot sits on the head axis. Below, the efficiency hump on the same flow scale, with a marker at this flow.

pages.name: The water's power
pages.task: At friction ×2, the pump gives about 11.2 L/s of seawater at 25 m. What power does the water take?
pages.why: The water takes ρgQH, with Q in m³/s. 11.2 L/s is 0.0112 m³/s. So 1025 × 9.81 × 0.0112 × 25 is about 2.8 kW. That is less than the 3.13 kW with the valve open. The flow fell by about a fifth, but the head rose by only about a seventh.

pages.name: Slowing the pump
pages.text: A slower pump has a lower curve. The [[pump laws]] say the flow goes with the speed, the head with the speed squared and the power with the speed cubed. At 80% the top falls to 30 × 0.8² = 19.2 m. Slowing the pump cuts the flow without burning head in a valve. The faint dot is the same pump at full speed, throttled instead. It is shown at 80%.
pages.alt: A graph of head against flow, with the pump's curve and the system curve. A dot marks where they cross, the operating point, with dashed guides to the axes. A second dot marks full speed with the valve at friction ×4. Below, the efficiency hump on the same flow scale, with a marker at this flow.

pages.name: Too slow
pages.task: The pump is slowed to 55%. Its most head is now 30 × 0.55², about 9.1 m. The lift is 10 m. What flow does it give?
pages.why: Even at no flow, the pump gives only 9.1 m. The pipe needs 10 m before any water moves. So its whole curve sits under the system curve, and nothing flows. With a lift, the flow falls faster than the speed.
pages.alt: A graph of head against flow: the full-speed pump curve, the system curve from the 10 m lift, and a dot on the head axis at 9.1 m, the 55% pump's most head. The 55% curve lies wholly under the system curve: they never cross.

pages.name: Suction and cavitation
pages.text: Water boils at 100 °C at normal pressure, and cooler at lower pressure. Each pump needs a least absolute pressure at its inlet. That is its [[NPSH required]], or net positive suction head. The pressure falls further on the way into the impeller's eye. What the suction offers, NPSH available, must be more. Both tanks move together, so only the suction changes. It is shown at −4 m.

pages.name: Stopping the cavitation
pages.task: The tank is at −4 m, with the valve open, and the pump cavitates. Which one stops it?
pages.why: Cavitation rattles and can pit the impeller, so it is worth stopping. Raising the tank adds its height to what the suction offers. At −3 m, about 5.6 m is available, above the 5.0 m required. A suction valve's friction comes off what is available. A faster pump needs more.

pages.name: A positive displacement pump
pages.text: A [[positive displacement pump]] traps a set volume each turn and pushes it on. So its speed sets its flow. A little slips back past it, more as the head climbs. So its curve stands nearly upright. From open to friction ×10, its flow barely moves, while its head and power climb steeply. The picture shows this pump at friction ×10.

pages.name: Left running shut
pages.task: A centrifugal pump runs on against a shut valve. Its shaft puts 3.0 kW into the 5 kg of seawater trapped in its casing. It takes 3850 J to warm 1 kg of seawater by 1 °C. How fast does the water warm?
pages.why: Use Q = mcΔT for each second. The warming is 3,000 ÷ (5 × 3850), about 0.16 °C a second. That is near 9 °C a minute. Water boils at 100 °C at normal pressure, and cooler at lower pressure. So the warmer the water, the higher the pressure it boils at. NPSH available falls, and the pump heads for cavitation.

pages.name: Reading the gauges
pages.task: A centrifugal fire pump's outlet gauge reads higher than usual. Its ammeter and its flow read lower. What is most likely?
pages.answer: Something on the discharge side is choking it
pages.why: Higher head with less flow means the dot has moved up the pump's curve. A steeper system curve does that. So something on the discharge side is choking the flow, such as a valve on the fire main left partly shut. Less flow on this pump means less current too.
pages.alt: A graph of head against flow: the pump's curve, the usual system curve and the usual operating point. A steeper system curve moves the dot up the pump's curve, to less flow and more head.
options: A discharge valve has been opened further
Something on the discharge side is choking it

pages.name: A higher tank
pages.task: The high tank is raised 6 m, so the lift is 16 m on the same pipe. Where does the pump settle?
pages.why: Set the two heads equal. 30 − 0.04q² = 16 + 0.06q², so 0.1q² = 14 and q² = 140. That gives about 11.8 L/s, at 30 − 0.04 × 140 = 24.4 m.
pages.alt: A graph of head against flow: the pump's curve, the old system curve from the 10 m lift, and a dashed line at the new 16 m lift. The new system curve crosses the pump's at about 11.8 L/s and 24.4 m.
